PS-1

Approvals, site layout and project duration

Paperwork with the local body and RERA, a site layout for labour housing, material storage and offices, and the total number of working days.

1Problem statement

Theme: complete all paperwork related to the local governing body and RERA, develop a detailed site layout for efficient circulation of labour housing, material storage and civil site office, and determine the total duration of the project.

Your company has just won a contract for the construction of a shopping mall. There are 7 blocks with interconnected pathways and 3 stories of underground parking. The preliminary estimate is about 12,000 m³ of concrete. The blocks are built on 8 acres (existing ground drawing in AutoCAD provided). You receive the mobilisation amount in the next week.

  • Study all paperwork required by the local governing body and RERA. Contact the Architect, Structural Engineer and MEP Engineer for the required permissions.
  • Provide stay for all skilled and unskilled labour, following the Government of India guidelines that apply once labour crosses a certain limit.
  • Check whether the concrete quantity justifies your own concrete plant or whether RMC will suffice. If a plant is set up, find raw material vendors, choose a location from which concrete reaches all corners, and work out the conveying systems.
  • Provide separate lots for carpenters and fabricators with material storage.
  • Provide the electrical and water requirements for the site and labour camp.
  • Provide a civil engineering site office and a sales office. There are 2 gates for entrance and exit.
  • Set up a material testing lab and store.
  • Determine the probable number of working days for completion.

B. Labour housing and statutory guidelines

The four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025, so the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (OSH) Code now covers building and construction work, with Central Rules notified in 2026. Welfare duties grow with the number of workers on site.

  • Register the establishment and make sure every labour contractor holds a licence.
  • Provide drinking water, separate latrines and urinals for men and women, a rest shelter, first-aid box and trained first aider on site.
  • Provide a canteen and crèche once the worker or women-worker numbers cross the limits in the Rules. Confirm those limits in the current Central Rules.
  • Appoint a safety officer and form a safety committee when the headcount crosses the limit in the Rules.
  • Working week is capped at 48 hours, overtime is paid at double the normal rate, and building workers aged 40 or more get a free annual health check.
  • Migrant workers need the journey and displacement provisions that now sit inside the OSH Code.

AssumptionPeak headcount of about 240 workers (worked out in PS-5) at 4 m² of dormitory per person gives about 960 m². Adding 40% for kitchen, toilets, crèche, first aid and recreation gives a camp of about 1,350 m², placed in the north-east corner away from public frontage, the batching plant and the haul road.

B2. Welfare provisions studied for Review 1

Construction workers must be given temporary accommodation and welfare facilities at or near the worksite: suitable accommodation, separate cooking, bathing and washing areas, adequate toilets and urinals, safe drinking water kept away from sanitary facilities, first aid and, where applicable, a crèche. These provisions aim at safe, hygienic and healthy living.

The Review 1 slides cite the BOCW Act, 1996 (Section 32 drinking water, Section 33 latrines and urinals, Section 34 accommodation) and the Karnataka BOCW Rules, 2006. Those duties now sit inside the OSH Code, as explained in section B.

C. RMC or our own concrete plant

FactorRMC onlyOwn batching plant
VolumeNo capital cost. Fits a 12,000 m³ project.Setup cost is spread over only 12,000 m³, so savings per m³ must be large enough to repay it.
Peak poursSupplier fleet can cover a raft pour of 500 to 800 m³ in a day.A 30 m³/h plant gives about 300 m³ in a 10-hour day, so big raft pours still need RMC.
Quality controlControl sits with the supplier. Site checks the delivery docket and slump.Full control and traceability of cement, aggregate and admixture batches.
ReliabilityExposed to traffic, monsoon and the supplier's other customers.On-site supply, independent of road delays.
Lead timeAvailable from day one.Setup, power and licence take weeks, so RMC is needed at the start.
Break-even volume N = F ÷ (R − C) | F: plant setup, dismantling and staff cost · R: RMC delivered rate per m³ · C: own variable cost per m³

Recommendation: use both. Pour the raft and basement with RMC while the plant is set up, then run a 30 m³/h plant for the superstructure and use RMC to top up large pours. If the quotes show N is more than the volume the plant would supply (about 6,000 m³), drop the plant and stay with RMC. Replace R and C with real quotes before deciding.

  • 20 mm and 10 mm aggregate: licensed crushers around Hubballi-Dharwad
  • Sand: licensed M-sand or crushed sand units
  • Admixtures and fly ash or GGBS
What to compare

  • Daily supply capacity and credit terms
  • Distance to site, so no truck takes more than the haul time allowed
  • Get three quotes for each material
Conveying concrete
  • Transit mixers on the one-way haul loop
  • Two stationary or boom pumps, so no pipeline is longer than about 150 m
  • Tower cranes with hoppers for isolated or small pours
  • Line pump down the ramp for basements

D. Site layout

Blocks (3-level basement runs beneath blocks and pathways)Site facilitiesLabour campOrange arrows: one-way truck loop

Schematic, not to scale.

  • Gate 1 is the truck entrance, Gate 2 is the truck exit. Trucks run a one-way loop. Gate 2 also carries the pedestrian lane for labour, staff and visitors, kept apart from trucks by a barrier.
  • The store and test lab sit side by side next to Gate 1, so a delivery is checked a few metres from where it enters.
  • The batching plant, steel yard and carpentry yard sit on the west spine, so concrete, bars and shuttering all start near the entrance and move by the loop road, pumps and tower cranes.
  • The labour camp is in the far corner, away from dust, trucks and public view, with its own path to Gate 2.
  • The sales office faces the road side at Gate 2, away from construction traffic.
  • Haul roads are 6 to 7 m wide with a turning radius of about 12 m for transit mixers. Fire hydrant ring and an assembly point go on the open ground beside the blocks.

What I observed

Add your own observations for this site: gate layout, material storage, internal roads and temporary facilities.

LessonA small, tight site pushes storage and labour housing off site (Visit 1). A larger RERA-registered project is expected to keep its approvals in order (Visit 2). For the mall I keep storage, labour camp and gates inside the 8 acres and keep an approvals register on site.

4Reflection

I started this problem thinking a site layout was a drawing exercise. It turned out to be a set of choices that pull against each other. The batching plant wants to be near the gate and near the blocks, while the labour camp wants distance from both. The approvals list was the second surprise. The K-RERA registration, the fire NOC and the labour licences each block a different activity, and one missing paper can stop a whole phase. Next time I would start the approvals tracker first and draw the layout second.

5Conclusion

The 7-block, 12,000 m³ project needs approvals running in parallel with mobilisation, a camp of about 1,350 m² for roughly 240 workers, and a one-way haul loop between two gates. A hybrid of RMC and a 30 m³/h plant suits the volume, because the plant cannot cover raft pours and RMC is needed on day one. Under the stated assumptions the job needs about 665 working days, or 26 months.

PS-2

Material procurement, QC and stores

A system that a new store manager can run with minimum supervision from the project manager.

1Problem statement

Theme: develop a system for construction material procurement, QC, storage and accounts which can be sustainable with minimum supervision from the project manager.

As the project manager, you have just hired a new store manager who lacks the experience for large-scale projects. The project starts in 15 days. Set up a material procurement system which can sustain with your minimum involvement once the project starts. The system must meet these conditions:

  • Prepare the layout of the store keeping in mind consumables, non-consumables, equipment and safety gear.
  • The site has 2 gates. Based on the store location, decide which gate is for ingress and which for departure.
  • All vehicle numbers must be recorded when they enter and exit the site, using the security and technology at your disposal.
  • The driver must bring the invoice. One copy stays with security, one with the store manager and one goes to the accounts section.
  • Materials must pass quality checks with the QA/QC inspector working with the store manager, keeping the material testing lab close to the store. Rejected material leaves the premises immediately, with proper paperwork.
  • Accepted material goes to its designated storage slot as defined during site layout planning.

3Solutions

A. Store layout

Covered store · consumablesCement on pallets, binding wire, nails, curing compound, admixtures, welding rods, cutting discs.
Issue counterOne window, one register. Nothing leaves without an issue slip.
PPEHelmets, shoes, harness, gloves.
Non-consumablesProps, plates, hand tools, shuttering accessories. Each tagged and signed out.
Equipment bayVibrators, bar cutters, welding sets, pumps. Log of issue and return.
QC bayInspection table, sample bags.
Open baysAggregates, sand and blocks in partitioned bays.
Steel racksRacks by diameter on sleepers. Covered. Link to the steel yard.
Reject yardTagged area by the exit road. Nothing stays more than a day.
PlacementThe store sits beside the test lab, a short walk from Gate 1 (see the PS-1 layout).
  • Cement is stacked on pallets clear of the floor and walls, no more than 10 bags high, and issued first in, first out by batch.
  • Every item has a bin card at its location showing opening stock, receipts, issues and balance.

B. Gate use

Gate 1 is ingress, Gate 2 is departure. The store and the lab are next to Gate 1, so loaded trucks reach them without crossing the site. Empty and rejected trucks leave by Gate 2 through a one-way loop, so incoming and outgoing vehicles never meet.

C. Receiving process

Step 1Vehicle arrives at Gate 1. Number is read by camera or entered on a QR gate pass. Time in is logged.
Step 2Security checks invoice and challan against the purchase order and keeps copy 1.
Step 3Loaded vehicle is weighed in (bulk items) and sent to the store bay.
Step 4Store manager takes copy 2, counts, and calls the QA/QC inspector.
Step 5Inspector checks the item. Pass: stored in its slot, receipt note raised. Fail: reject tag and rejection note.
Step 6Rejected load leaves at once by Gate 2 with the rejection note. Weight out and time out are logged.
Step 7Copy 3, receipt note and inspection report go to accounts within 24 hours. Accounts matches order, receipt and invoice before paying.

Vehicle log fields: date, vehicle number, supplier, material, challan number, time in, time out, weight in and out, receiving store person. A shared spreadsheet or form on a phone is enough, and the camera read plus QR pass avoids typing errors.

D. Quality checks at receipt

MaterialCheck at the storeReject if
CementBrand, grade, ISI mark, batch number, date of packing, bag weight, no lumpsOld stock, torn bags, hardened lumps, short weight
Reinforcement steelGrade (Fe 500D), mill test certificate, diameter, weight per metre, rust, bend test sampleNo certificate, under-weight, heavy scaling
Aggregates and sandVisual grading, silt, moisture, sample sent to lab for sieve analysisDirty, wrong size, high silt
Blocks and bricksSize, shape, breakage count, compressive strength sampleExcess breakage, low strength
RMC (when used)Delivery docket, batch time, slump, temperatureOver the time limit, wrong grade, wrong slump

E. Running it with minimum supervision

Reorder level = daily use × supplier lead time + safety stock | Steel example: 4.5 t/day × (7 + 3 days) = 45 t
  • Delegated limits. The store manager raises purchase requests only up to the reorder level. Anything above a set rupee value, or a new supplier, goes to the project manager.
  • Records. Purchase order, gate register, receipt note, inspection report, rejection note, issue slip, bin card and a stock ledger.
  • Daily one-page report to the project manager: receipts, rejections, issues, stock below reorder level.
  • Weekly physical count of fast movers (cement, steel) against the ledger, and a monthly full audit by someone outside the store.

4Reflection

A store runs well when the rules are on paper and the paper is simple. Coloured invoice copies, a reject tag and a reorder level take a new store manager a day to learn, and they replace a hundred daily questions to the project manager. The hardest part is discipline at the gate, because that is where shortcuts start.

5Conclusion

Gate 1 for entry and Gate 2 for exit, a lab beside the store, three copies of every invoice, a documented accept-or-reject decision and reorder levels give a store that can be run by a new manager. The project manager reads one daily report and steps in only for exceptions.

PS-3

Survey plan and outsourced work

Benchmarks, a visit plan that limits the consultant's cost, and the reasons for outsourcing survey work.

1Problem statement

Theme: develop a surveying plan for a particular site and a system to manage in-house engineers and outsourced work.

Project execution starts in 5 days. The survey work is outsourced to a Bengaluru-based surveying consultant. Their team, equipped with a total station, will travel to Hubballi for the permanent benchmark location and marking. Using the site layout plan, mark the important benchmark locations throughout the site and mark the RLs when the surveying team arrives. The team charges Rs. 10,000 plus travel and stay expenses every time they come to the site. Plan the surveying work to minimise expenses.

Furthermore, if your site has qualified civil engineers, why did your company outsource the surveying work? Brainstorm the possible reasons.

3Solutions

A. Benchmarks and control points

▲ Temporary benchmark (TBM)Control point (CP) for the building gridDashed box: excavation limit

Schematic, not to scale.

  • Six TBMs on the boundary, outside the zone of influence of the deep excavation, so they do not settle or get disturbed. Concrete pillar with a steel pin, painted and fenced.
  • Four control points at the corners of the footprint to hold the building grid, each with offset reference marks outside the dig.
  • Every TBM is checked against the others by closed levelling loops. Any one that disagrees is rejected.
PointLocation
TBM1North-west boundary
TBM2North boundary, mid-point
TBM3North-east boundary
TBM4South-east boundary
TBM5South boundary, mid-point
TBM6South-west boundary

B. Visit plan to keep cost down

Hubballi is about 400 km from Bengaluru, an overnight trip each way, so travel and stay cost more than the fee. The consultant sets accurate control once, and the in-house engineers do daily setting out from it with an auto level and theodolite.

VisitWhenWork done
1Before excavation (day 5)Boundary check, benchmark transfer, six TBMs with RL, four control points, excavation limit marked
2Excavation near formation levelVerify depth and control, mark raft and column grid for the basement
3Before ground-floor columnsRe-establish grid at ground level, check verticality datum
4Before superstructure of the first blocksTransfer grid, check TBMs for settlement
5CompletionAs-built survey and final levels
Cost = visits × (10,000 + travel and stay T) | 5 visits: 50,000 + 5T against a monthly visit over 26 months: 2,60,000 + 26T

Planned visits save at least 2,10,000 + 21T, where T is the cost of one trip. Add a call-out only if a TBM is disturbed.

C. Managing in-house engineers and the consultant

  • Roles. Consultant: control, grid and as-built. Site engineers: daily setting out, level checks, record keeping. Project manager: approves requests for extra visits.
  • Survey register for every setting-out job: date, drawing revision, who set out, who checked, tolerance.
  • Hold point. No footing, column or slab pour is released without a signed survey clearance.
  • Handover. The consultant leaves the control sheet, coordinates and RLs, which the team treats as the only valid reference.

D. Why outsource when the site has qualified civil engineers

Accuracy and equipment
  • A calibrated total station and a trained surveyor give tighter control than a site engineer's day-to-day kit.
  • Owning and calibrating one is costly and idle most of the time.
Independence
  • A third party checks the contractor's own work, so errors are not hidden.
  • The record carries weight in disputes with the client or neighbours.
Specialist skill
  • Benchmark transfer, closed traverses and boundary verification are a specialist task.
  • Needed only a few times, so hiring full-time does not pay.
Time and risk
  • Site engineers are busy with quality, labour and billing.
  • The consultant carries the liability for the control accuracy.

4Reflection

My first reaction to outsourcing was that a qualified site engineer could do the survey. The reasons are accuracy, independence and equipment, not skill. I also saw that cost is mostly decided by how many times the team travels, so the visit plan matters more than the day rate.

5Conclusion

Six boundary TBMs and four control points, set once by the consultant and used by the site team for daily work, with five planned visits instead of monthly ones. Outsourcing gives accuracy, an independent record and specialist skill at a cost the project can control.

PS-4

Reducing steel and formwork wastage

BBS, ordering, storage, reconciliation and a reuse routine that cut wastage from 12% to 5% for steel and by 4% for plywood.

1Problem statement

Theme: reduce wastage of steel and formwork through efficient management.

Your company's historical data shows an average steel wastage of 12% and plywood-for-formwork wastage of about 9%. Excavation is in progress for the next 30 days. Use this time to develop a system with considerable control over:

  • The calculation of steel required (BBS)
  • The process of ordering the steel (project-wise or block-wise)
  • Storage and releasing it to the fabricators
  • Reconciliation

Plan and execute your system to bring the wastage of steel down to 5%.

A similar system is to be set up for formwork (reduce wastage by 4%):

  • Figure out the different groups of columns and beams based on size.
  • Set up a working procedure to reuse a set of formwork a minimum of 10 times.

3Solutions

A. What the target is worth

ItemAt 12%At 5%Basis
Steel needed (theoretical)1,320 t1,320 t12,000 m³ × 110 kg per m³
Wastage158.4 t66.0 t1,320 t × 12% and × 5%
Steel saved92.4 tAbout Rs. 55 lakh at Rs. 60,000 per tonne

Assumption110 kg of steel per m³ and Rs. 60,000 per tonne are placeholders. Use the structural engineer's quantity and the current rate.

B. Where steel is lost and how each loss is controlled

Source of lossControl
Cutting offcutsCutting plan that combines bar lengths on 12 m stock. Example: 3 pieces of 3.1 m and 1 of 2.4 m use 11.7 m, a loss of only 0.3 m (2.5%). Offcuts are reused for spacers and chairs.
Over-orderingOrders are drawn from the BBS for one block and one pour cycle, not from estimates.
Drawing revisionsBBS carries the drawing revision number. A new revision cancels the old schedule.
Rust and damageRacks off the ground, covered, first in first out.
Unrecorded issue or theftSteel is issued only against a signed bar cutting schedule, and offcuts come back to the store by weight.
Extra laps and wrong sizesStandard lap lengths, couplers for large diameters, mill certificate and weight check at receipt.

C. The four controls

BBS
  • Prepared per element from good-for-construction drawings
  • Bar marks and shapes per IS 2502
  • Checked by a second engineer before release
Ordering
  • Rate contract for the whole project to lock price
  • Block-wise call-offs in 12 m lengths by diameter
  • 7 to 10 days of lead time built into the schedule

Why both: project-wise buying gets a better rate, block-wise delivery keeps stock short and reconciliation simple.

Storage and release
  • Racks by diameter on sleepers, ends painted per grade
  • Issue slip against the bar cutting schedule
  • Cut and bent bars tagged with bar mark and block
Reconciliation
  • Weekly per block and element
  • Offcuts weighed and returned
  • Anything over 5% triggers a review
Wastage % = (steel issued − theoretical weight from BBS) ÷ theoretical weight × 100 | Issued = fixed + scrap + returned

D. Formwork: groups and reuse

Wastage of 9% is read as a target of 5%, a reduction of four percentage points. Fewer sizes mean panels can be reused across floors and blocks.

GroupSize (mm), exampleNotes
Column C-A300 × 600Merge sizes within 25 mm where the structural engineer approves
Column C-B450 × 450Common in the basement levels
Column C-C450 × 750Panel sets shared across blocks
Column C-D600 × 600Steel or phenolic-faced ply for heavy reuse
Beam B-A230 × 450Partition-wall beams
Beam B-B300 × 600Typical floor beams
Beam B-C400 × 900Transfer and large-span beams

ExampleThese sizes show the method. Group the sizes from your structural drawings.

Step 1Cut panels to standard sizes on a cutting plan for 8 ft × 4 ft sheets.
Step 2Seal edges, apply release agent, mark each panel with an ID and reuse count.
Step 3Erect with clamps and wedges. No nails through the face.
Step 4Strip after the permitted time, using wedges, never crowbars on the face.
Step 5Clean, inspect, repair edges, and tick the reuse count.
Step 6Stack flat under cover. Retire at 10 uses or when the face fails, and reuse as secondary shuttering.

AssumptionWith 7 m² of formwork per m³ of concrete, 12,000 m³ needs 84,000 m² of contact area. At 10 reuses that is 8,400 m² of plywood, about 2,820 sheets of 2,440 × 1,220 mm. Wastage of 9% against 5% is about 254 sheets against 141, a saving of about 113 sheets.

4Reflection

Most steel wastage is decided before a bar is cut: in the BBS, in the order and in the cutting plan. Reconciliation shows whether the plan was followed. Formwork follows the same logic. Standard sizes and care when stripping decide whether plywood lasts four pours or ten.

5Conclusion

A checked BBS, block-wise call-offs under a project rate contract, issue only against cutting schedules and weekly reconciliation can bring steel wastage from 12% to 5%, about 92 tonnes on this project. Standard formwork groups and a ten-use handling routine bring plywood wastage from 9% to 5%.

PS-5

Optimum labour force by stage

Skilled and unskilled headcount through the stages of construction, wages and the labour contract.

1Problem statement

Theme: determine the optimum labour force through the various stages of construction.

The concrete required for each block can be obtained from the quantity take-off. Based on the given numbers, work out the number of skilled labour (fabricators, carpenters, masons) and the number of unskilled labour (usually called the concrete gang).

  • There will be a peak time during execution where a large number of labour is required, and slack time when a smaller number will suffice.
  • If you hire less labour, productivity will suffer.
  • If you hire more labour, you will not have enough work to engage them and they will leave.
  • You should have all the prevailing wages in your area and the minimum wage specified by the government.
  • Your company must sign a contract with the labour supplier. You should know all the legal and technical details of such a contract.

B. How the numbers were worked out

AssumptionProductivity norms to calibrate on site: bar benders cut and bend 200 kg per day, fixers place 250 kg per day, carpenters erect 8 m² of formwork per day, a concrete gang of 15 to 20 handles a pour at 40 m³/h. Steel is 110 kg per m³, so about 1,320 t, split 45% basement and 55% superstructure. Formwork is about 5 m² per m³ in the basement and 7 m² per m³ above.

  • Fabricators. Basement steel of 594 t over 150 days is 3,960 kg per day: 20 benders and 16 fixers, about 35. Superstructure steel of 726 t over 160 days is 4,540 kg per day: 23 benders and 18 fixers, about 40.
  • Carpenters. Superstructure formwork of 38,500 m² over 160 days is about 240 m² per day. At 8 m² per carpenter that is 30, and about 35 with stripping and shifting.
  • Unskilled. A concrete gang of about 30 for large pours plus helpers for steel, shuttering and curing.

The peak is short, so the extra 60 workers should come as a second gang on a short contract rather than as permanent hires. In slack months, release the unskilled helpers first and keep the skilled gangs together.

Skilled MEP and finishing trades come through their own subcontractors and are on top of these numbers.

D. Wages

The Code on Wages applies, and Karnataka reported a revised minimum wage notification on 22 May 2026 for 81 scheduled employments, with rates by skill level and zone. The construction rate for Hubballi-Dharwad comes from the official schedule, and the company pays the higher of that and the local market rate for each trade (mason, carpenter, bar bender, helper).

E. Contract with the labour supplier

Legal
  • Valid contractor licence under the OSH Code
  • PF and ESIC registration, wages at or above the minimum
  • Wage payment date and the principal employer's liability if the contractor defaults
  • Insurance for injury or death
  • No child or bonded labour
  • Hours, overtime, migrant provisions, welfare and housing
Technical
  • Scope, trades and gang sizes
  • Rate per day or per unit of work, and how measured
  • Productivity and quality standards, with rework at the contractor's cost
  • Mobilisation date and replacement of non-performing gangs
  • Who supplies tools and PPE
Commercial
  • Retention or security deposit
  • Penalty for absenteeism or delay
  • Termination and notice period
  • Dispute resolution by arbitration
  • Stamp duty and signed copies on file

CheckGet the final contract wording reviewed by the company's legal or HR team before signing.

4Reflection

Hiring labour is a balance between productivity and idle time. A headcount chart drawn against the pour schedule makes the trade-off visible. The contract matters as much as the number, because wages, licences and welfare become the principal employer's problem if the supplier fails.

5Conclusion

Labour rises from about 57 at set-up to 180 in the superstructure and about 240 at the short peak overlap, then falls to 50 at handover. A core of skilled gangs held together, a second gang for the peak and a signed contract covering wages, licences and welfare keep productivity up without idle labour.

PS-6

Site tests and failed concrete cubes

Why 23 of 56 columns failed the 28-day test while all 106 footings passed, and how to stop it happening again.

1Problem statement

Theme: demonstrate the importance of various tests conducted on site and the ramifications of the failure of material tests.

RCC work is in progress and has reached ground floor level in 3 blocks. Concrete cubes cast during the RCC work of all footings and columns are sent for testing by a third-party testing company. Out of 106 footings cast, all 106 attained the required strength. But out of 56 columns cast, 23 failed the 28-day compressive strength test. Since your own concrete plant is still being set up, you used local RMC for this work. The RMC owner has a clause in the contract that any failure of strength attainment is his responsibility and he will bear the expenses to demolish the failed structural component and rebuild it. This clause saved a lot of financial loss to your company. But the RMC contractor still says there was a mistake in the concreting at the site.

Brainstorm to figure out all the possibilities that might have gone wrong. Develop a plan that will ensure no concrete cube test fails in this project hereafter. Also, from the RMC owner's point of view, what precautions should he take to avoid such conditions in the future?

2Minutes of meeting

Add the meeting photo here

  • How cubes are cast, marked, cured and sent to the lab.

Add the meeting photo here

Meeting 2 · RMC plant representative

Date
[dd/mm/yyyy]
Time
[hh:mm]
Venue
[place]

Points discussed

  • Mix design, batching control and moisture correction.
  • Delivery time limits, slump and what happens when water is added at site.
  • Contract clause on strength failure and how disputes are handled.

3Solutions

A. Read the pattern first

All 106 footings passed and 23 of 56 columns failed, which is 41% of columns. The same RMC and the same lab produced both, so the useful question is what differs for columns. Columns are narrow, heavily reinforced, tall, often a higher grade, and poured from a greater height.

Before blaming anyone, tabulate each failed column by pour date, truck, mix grade, column height, who cast the cubes and the cube set. If the failures cluster on one date or one plant batch, the cause is in supply. If they spread across dates but share a handling step, the cause is on site or in the lab.

B. What could have gone wrong

Mix and materials
  • Water-cement ratio too high
  • Poor batching or no moisture correction
  • Low-grade cement, dirty aggregate
  • Admixture dose wrong or wrong type
  • Different mix design for columns, with a higher grade not achieved
Transport and delay
  • Long haul or waiting time, so slump loss
  • Water added at site to restore workability
  • Hot weather without retarder
Placing and compaction
  • Drop height too high, causing segregation
  • Poor compaction in congested bars
  • Honeycombing at the base
  • Leaking formwork losing paste
Curing
  • Columns not cured, or cured late
  • Hot sun and wind on exposed faces
Sampling and cube handling
  • Cubes taken from the last of the load, or from a different batch
  • Cubes poorly compacted
  • Left in the sun or moved within the first 24 hours
  • Not cured in water at 27 ± 2 °C
Testing and records
  • Machine not calibrated or loading rate wrong
  • Cubes mislabelled between footings and columns
  • Wrong grade used for acceptance

A failed cube is not yet a failed column. Cubes test the sample, not the structure. Before any demolition, test the columns with rebound hammer and ultrasonic pulse velocity, then cut cores. Under IS 456, cores are acceptable if their average is at least 85% of the specified strength and no single core is below 75%.

C. Plan so that no cube fails again

StageControl
Before the pourApproved mix design and trial mixes for each grade. Pre-pour checklist: formwork tight, cover blocks, bars clean, pump and labour ready, curing arrangements ready. No pour on a day the supplier or the crew cannot support.
At deliveryCheck the docket for grade, batch time and quantity. Measure slump and temperature on every truck. Reject loads over the time limit (typically 2 hours, less in hot weather) or outside the slump range. No water added at site without the engineer's written approval.
PlacingLimit free fall, use tremie or chute for tall columns, place in layers and compact with needle vibrators. Check the base for honeycombing at stripping.
SamplingTake cubes from the middle of the discharge, in the engineer's presence. Casting frequency follows IS 456: 1 sample for 1 to 5 m³, rising to 4 samples at 31 to 50 m³, and one more for every extra 50 m³ or part of it. Each sample is 3 cubes. Cast cubes in clean oiled moulds and mark them with element, date and truck.
Cube careKeep them still and shaded for 24 hours, de-mould, and cure in clean water at 27 ± 2 °C. Run 7-day tests as an early warning, so a problem shows after a week and not after a month.
Curing the structureStart curing as soon as the surface can take it. Wet hessian or ponding on columns for the specified days, with a signed curing log.
LabUse an accredited lab with a calibrated machine, and send a duplicate set to a second lab for key elements.
RecordsOne register per pour: element, grade, truck, slump, temperature, cube IDs, 7-day and 28-day results. Review the running average of results weekly against the acceptance rule.

The acceptance rule in IS 456 requires the mean of a group of results to exceed the specified strength by a margin and no single result to fall more than 3 N/mm² below it. Any drift in the running average is acted on before a failure.

D. What the RMC owner should do

  • Keep calibrated batching equipment and correct for aggregate moisture at every batch.
  • Re-verify mix designs regularly and when cement or aggregate source changes, and test cubes at the plant on every grade.
  • Print a batch ticket for every truck with batch time, grade and water, and keep retained samples of cement and admixture.
  • Dispatch only when the site is ready, and set a delivery time limit in the contract.
  • Add retarder in hot weather and keep transit mixers clean.
  • Write contract terms that fix responsibility at the point of discharge, require joint sampling, name an accredited lab and state that water added at site without written approval voids the guarantee.
  • Send a technician to critical pours and keep photos of slump tests and sampling.
  • Insure the supply and keep a record of strength results to show that the plant is in statistical control.

4Reflection

The footings passed and the columns did not, so the useful question was what differs between them. Narrow sections, congested bars, drop height, higher grade and cube handling all point to the columns. I also learned that a failed cube is not yet a failed column, and that the core test decides that. The RMC clause protected the company financially, but it does not replace our own checks.

5Conclusion

Columns failed where footings passed, which points to mix, placing, curing and cube handling rather than a general supply failure. Pattern analysis, then NDT and cores, should come before any demolition. A pre-pour checklist, slump and temperature on every truck, controlled sampling, 7-day checks and a pour register prevent repeats, and a plant with batch records and clear contract terms protects the RMC supplier.
